questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The availability of a strong program in my desired field. A culture that I was interested in exploring.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The exchange program at UoC is very well run and quite organised, even if information sometimes would come slightly later than I was expecting, I was at no point forgotten.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: E-mail introduction, offer to help set-up student ID. Offer to have an intro meeting at exchange office.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Not very easy to find cheap housing. Facebook is an option, and one i should probably have used. 
I did Airbnb and lived in an absolute perfect place but at a slightly over budget rate.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Heraklion is very well connected by private public busses. It’s easy to get around, and the entire city feels very student friendly and filled with student life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I received temporary papers automatically and was easily temporarily registered. Getting an actual student ID, turned out to be a little difficult and required a Greek SIM card and going to a Vodafone shop, eventually I gave up and used my temporary papers.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Quick response from the exchange office, which was in general excellent.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
NA
I was registered for my clinical rotations from home, and it could have been tweaked a little, but overall there were no issues.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to connect with people who have exchanged to UoC before, or even try to get in touch with local students. The departments are very different and it’s not obvious in what ways from reading about them.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Clinical rotations so not really courses. 
The theoretical level compared to KU is quite high. As an 11th semester student the level of independence and amount of practical work was lower compared to home. Generally speaking less independence and preparation for practicing alone and more focus on teaching skills and knowledge in the clinic under supervision.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
As above, with the caveat that the difference from department to department was very large. 
Generally more 1 to 1 with the same doctor over extended periods of time.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Rotations in 
Internal medicine 
Anaesthesiology 
Rheumatology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All rotations have my warm recommendation, but anaesthesiology would be absolutely amazing for anyone interested in doing it. 
Very hands on, a very good culture in the department, general culture not too dissimilar from home, but with options to do a lot of hands on work. 
Rheumatology was a specialised department with a high degree of research activity, and quite broad patient base. 
Internal medicine would be useful for practicing clinical skills and theory especially as an early clinical experience, but older patient population means Greek language knowledge would have been useful to work more independently.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Housing more expensive. 
Social life, and seeing the surrounding areas less expensive

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Different social clubs: choir and chess to football. 
City has cheap gyms and football fields.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Everyone enjoyed the hiking club, from party people to outdoors people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Going camping in the south and east of Crete away from the most touristic places. 
Renting a car and going Roadtripping on the island. 
Hiking and mountain climbing. 
Island hopping to the neighbour islands. Social life in the city is very easy and fun.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
The culture is very very different, but people were friendly and used to having guests. 
Some things(like the shouting) never really settled. In general I was comfortable from day one though.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Get a WhatsApp group going with the other exchange students, more people find more social events. 
Spend some time at the hospital, the greek students have rotations of a month in each department, so you see the same faces every day. 
Use the buddy programme it worked well for some.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Greek people are very loud and sometimes shouting at each other mostly. 
That people are very often late without any explanation.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The openness and happiness to share. 
The pride in the work that is being done, and in being good at a task or sharing some knowledge.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Expect it to feel a little chaotic. 
Be patient. 
Try to keep up with Greek lessons, it is not impossible to learn some.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don’t be afraid to ask the exchange office.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The perspective it gave on what we do well and what we don’t do so well at home. And the appreciation of how good the system actually is at home, but how people can make things work in other ways, and that no place is perfect.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Language! 
I wish I had started studying harder and using it more early, because people will switch to their own language, and in the end of 14 weeks, even if you(as me) gave up early, at the end you will understand more than you think.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
I think the focus on basic skills make it a perfect 7th-8th semester exchange. It is very difficult to work independently, if you don’t speak Greek. However you will have more close supervision and more chances of practicing basic clinical skills and have at least as much theoretical teaching. You will get to test yourself in a different environment and you will get to present patients in a different way. 
The social life and free time will be awesome, and the people and the city is really nice. It will feel as a vacation even if you work as hard as at home. And it will be a more unique experience than going to a more “safe” Northern European university.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
